WOLF MERIDIAN GROUP LLC                                                               POWER | COMPUTE | INFRASTRUCTURE



                                BEFORE THE FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION
                                                    Docket No. AD26-8-000
                                   2026 Reliability Technical Conference | October 21, 2026

                                 WRITTEN COMMENTS OF JUSTIN TROUT
                   Strategic Infrastructure Planning, Large-Load Integration, and National Grid Security

Commissioners:
The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence, data centers, and other large electrical loads presents a challenge extending
beyond generation capacity. The United States is attempting to accommodate unprecedented computational demand
within an electrical system that was not designed around the geographic concentration, operating characteristics, or
infrastructure requirements of these emerging facilities.
My concern is that we continue addressing individual projects without adequately evaluating the cumulative
consequences for national infrastructure reliability and security.
Based on my research involving energy infrastructure, strategic site selection, and power-to-compute planning, I
respectfully submit four recommendations for consideration.
1. Establish a National Large-Load Site Readiness Framework.
Before committing to major computational developments, utilities and developers should evaluate actual deliverable
electrical capacity, transmission constraints, generation availability, substation capability, infrastructure upgrade
requirements, and realistic time-to-power. Proximity to existing transmission infrastructure must never be mistaken for
available capacity.
2. Prioritize Existing Infrastructure Before New Construction.
Former industrial facilities, energy-producing regions, brownfields, and underutilized industrial properties deserve
systematic evaluation. Where engineering assessments support reuse, existing infrastructure may reduce development
timelines, unnecessary duplication, environmental impacts, and costs ultimately borne by consumers.
3. Integrate National Security Into Reliability Planning.
Large-load integration introduces additional operational and security considerations. Planning should evaluate dynamic
load behavior, correlated outages, cybersecurity, physical protection, fuel availability, and interdependencies involving
water, communications, and essential services. Reliability cannot be measured solely by whether sufficient megawatts
exist under normal operating conditions.
4. Improve Coordination Across Energy, Technology, and Government.
Federal regulators, utilities, system operators, technology developers, and state authorities should adopt common
screening criteria and planning assumptions. These should address electrical capacity, water consumption, cooling
requirements, grid resilience, infrastructure investment, and the allocation of costs and operational risks.
Closing Recommendation
The Commission should consider advancing a coordinated, evidence-based framework for evaluating large
computational loads before development commitments create avoidable reliability problems.
The central question should not simply be how quickly America can build computational infrastructure, but whether
we are building it in locations our electrical system can responsibly and securely support.
Respectfully submitted,
Justin Trout, M.S.
Founder & Principal | Wolf Meridian Group LLC
www.wolfmeridian.com | jttrout38@gmail.com
